scopeNote: Read-only Sesotho body candidates for Water Harvesting L1, source-paired across all eight canonical paragraphs. The current ST registry holds the whole body in exact English, so there are no existing localized body paragraphs to preserve. Technical phrases for contour geometry, controlled grade, overflow, receiving points and earthworks are retained in English where a translation could change the design. No repository edits; candidates require independent Sesotho backcheck.

paragraphs.sourceEnglish: One kind of swale is a level trench on contour. It slows and spreads runoff so some water can soak into suitable soil. Other swales are designed with a slight, controlled grade to carry excess water slowly to a safe outlet. Which approach fits your land depends on the soil, slope, drainage and storm flow. Have a trained local adviser check the line, overflow and receiving point before digging.

sourceBody:
One kind of swale is a level trench on contour. It slows and spreads runoff so some water can soak into suitable soil. Other swales are designed with a slight, controlled grade to carry excess water slowly to a safe outlet. Which approach fits your land depends on the soil, slope, drainage and storm flow. Have a trained local adviser check the line, overflow and receiving point before digging.

The excavated soil forms a berm on the downhill side, where trees can be planted when the site design is suitable.

Trees planted there may draw on moisture stored in the soil after rain, depending on the site.

Heavy rain can fill a swale faster than water soaks into the soil. Plan a safe overflow before digging.

The route must not erode the slope or send damaging water to a neighbour. A downstream swale or dam must be able to receive it safely.

Ask a trained local adviser to assess the soil, slope and storm flow. A picture is not a construction design.

Slope alone does not tell you whether a swale is suitable. Soil, drainage, unstable ground and the water arriving from upslope all matter.

Keep good ground cover. Get a local assessment before digging on steep, wet or unstable land. Grass barriers and terraces also need a design suited to the site.

materialAmbiguities: The precise geometry of level contour and slight controlled grade is left in exact English in paragraph 1; do not wire a localized geometric paraphrase without specialist review.
Berm on the downhill side, safe outlet/overflow, and downstream receiving capacity retain English direction/design terms in paragraphs 1–5.
The infiltration wording in paragraphs 1 and 4 is an ordinary Sesotho attempt; a reviewer should confirm it means water soaking/entering the suitable soil and not necessarily all the runoff.
semanticChecks: All eight exact source paragraphs are represented in order; the current ST registry holds all eight in English, so there are no prior localized paragraphs to overwrite.
Level trench on contour remains distinguished from other swales designed with slight, controlled grade; excess water is carried slowly to a safe outlet only in the latter clause.
The trained local adviser checks the line, overflow and receiving point before digging; a later instruction also asks the trained adviser to assess soil, slope and storm flow.
Berm remains on the downhill side; tree planting and stored-soil-moisture benefits remain conditional on site design/site conditions.

Heavy-rain filling is a can-risk compared with infiltration; plan safe overflow before digging. The route must not erode the slope or send harmful water to a neighbour, and a downstream receiver must receive it safely.

Slope alone is insufficient; soil, drainage, unstable ground and water from upslope all matter. Steep, wet and unstable land require local assessment before digging; grass barriers and terraces need site-suited design.
uncertaintySummary: Unreviewed Sesotho machine draft, not fluent-speaker approval. Geometry, berm direction and safe outlet/overflow technical clauses remain English where translation could alter the earthwork. All eight body paragraphs were held English in the current ST registry; independent Sesotho and local earthworks review are required before wiring.

quizQuestions.sourceEnglish: A farmer planned a level contour swale. After heavy rain, one end holds most of the water. What should the farmer check before changing the earthwork?
quizQuestions.draft: Sehoai se ile sa rera level contour swale. Ka mora pula e matla, one end e holds most of the water. Sehoai se lokela ho hlahloba eng pele se fetola earthwork?
quizQuestions.literalBacktranslation: A farmer planned a level contour swale. After heavy rain, one end holds most of the water. What should the farmer check before changing the earthwork?
quizQuestions.uncertainty: Keeps the technical geometry, ‘holds most of the water’ comparison and earthwork term in English. Preserves the after-heavy-rain condition and asks what to check before any change.

quizQuestions.sourceEnglish: A farmer wants to control erosion on steep land. What should she do before digging?
quizQuestions.draft: Sehoai se batlang ho laola kgoholeho mobung o moepa se lokela ho etsa eng pele se tjheka?
quizQuestions.literalBacktranslation: A farmer who wants to control erosion on steep land should do what before digging?
quizQuestions.uncertainty: Preserves the steep-land condition and asks for action before digging; source does not specify the farmer's gender in Sesotho.

preservedHolds.sourceEnglish: A level contour swale can hold runoff for infiltration on a suitable site; other swales need a designed grade and safe outlet

A level contour design should spread water along its length. Uneven filling may indicate an unintended low point, but some swales are intentionally graded to a safe outlet. Check the actual design, soil and overflow route before altering it.
